Hallucinations are not mentioned therefore schizophrenia can be ruled out.Anxiety disorders are characterised by anticipatory anxiety, which is the fear of something happening without any evidence that it will. In PTSD the symptoms are triggered by cues from the trauma, such as loud noises or smells. Therefore the trigger here is being too close to the train line.Adjustment disorder is where there is a stressor but the symptoms are out of proportion to this. This would include Gemma disconnecting the cooker, however the other symptoms are more indicative of PTSD. The fact that the symptoms are triggered by cues from the trauma means that they cannot be classed as an adjustment disorder. The Flashbacks are also a key part of PTSD. The fact that she is hearing sounds of the past, indicates that she is experiencing hallucinations. This could be described as pseudohallucinations, where the patient hears things that aren't there. Her fear of the cooker, kettle and microwave are all examples of phobias. This is common in people with PTSD. The fact that she throws away the kettle shows that she has delusions. Delusion's are fixed beliefs that cannot be changed by logic or reason. PTSD can be caused by a wide range of events, including physical and sexual abuse, accidents, war/combat and natural disasters. It is thought to occur due to long term stress causing over activation of the HPA axis leading to down regulation of cortisol. This means that stress responses are less effective, so minor triggers cause the symptoms of PTSD. Treatment includes psychotherapy and medication, such as SSRI's and benzodiazepines. 3g of sodium chloride contains 1 molecule of Na+ and 2 molecules of Cl- therefore it will increase the plasma osmolality because Na+ is more concentrated in the serum than Cl-. This will stimulate the ADH receptors in the hypothalamus which will cause release of ADH from the posterior pituitary gland. The ADH then acts on collecting duct cells which causes them to insert aquaporins into their membranes which allows more water to be reabsorbed into circulation. This increases the GFR as more water is being removed by the glomeruli and this will lead to a rise in the blood pressure. The rise in blood pressure is sensed by the baroreceptors in the carotid sinus which will decrease ADH secretion. This means that the feedback loop between the baroreceptors and the hypothalamus is negative. 45 XO is the karyotype for Turner's syndrome. Turner's syndrome is associated with lymphedema (due to a lack of elastin), neck webbing, low-set ears, heart defects and primary amenorrhea. It is characterised by short stature due to poorly developed ovaries but does not affect IQ. Treatment for infertility involves assisted reproductive technology. Source: Karyotypes lecture from Case 7 Genetic Disorders plenary. See also http://www.genetics.uth.edu/resources/pp/turner.htm for more information on Turner's syndrome.  This question is essentially recalling a few facts about Turner's syndrome. The fact that Sarah had growth hormone treatment in childhood is a clue that it is unlikely to be 47 XYY or 47 XXY. Irritable bowel disease is associated with Turner's syndrome, along with other autoimmune diseases such as thyroiditis and diabetes mellitus type 1. Turner's syndrome is associated with primary amenorrhoea, however, if fertility treatment is successful, pregnancy can occur. Webbing of the neck is characteristic of 45 X. However, 45 X is not associated with a lack of elastin and so the presence of lymphedema rules out this option. Turner's syndrome is associated with a lack of elastin, so the presence of lymphedema and neck webbing would make Turner's syndrome the most likely diagnosis. The fact that Sarah is married makes trisomy 21 unlikely, although this could have been concealed.  Note that the fact that Sarah has these symptoms does not mean that she definitely has Turner's syndrome. There are plenty of other causes of short stature, amenorrhoea and irritable bowel disease. Osmotic diarrhoea is due to excess fluids being drawn into the colon due to too much fiber/water being absorbed in the upper GI tract. This means that osmotic diarrhoea is caused by anything that reduces absorption in the upper GI tract. Coeliac disease damages the villi in the small intestine and reduces absorption. It is a cause of malabsorption syndrome along with Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. Cholera and E.coli cause secretory diarrhoea which is due to excessive fluid production in the lumen of the bowel. This is because cholera produces a toxin which activates excessive Cl- channel activity in the apical membrane of enterocytes, drawing water into the lumen by osmosis. E.coli produces an enterotoxin which activates Cl- channels in the basal membrane of enterocytes, drawing water into the lumen of the bowel by osmosis. Giardia is a protozoa which causes diarrhoea due to a trophozoit migrating through the duodenum and attaching to the brush border of enterocytes. This causes increased paracellular absorption of sodium and water, leading to watery diarrhoea. Source: Case 10 lecture on 'Diarrhoea and Diarrhoeal Illnesses'. Instead, upon contact with the oocyte, the oocyte releases chemical signals which induce sperm to change direction and penetrate the zona pellucida (C). This occurs after capacitation (see B) as removing the glycoprotein coat allows the release of the enzymes Hyaluronidase and Acrosin from the sperm head. These act on the zona pellucida to allow sperm entry into the oocyte. Once inside the oocyte, the sperm then undergo further capacitation before the formation of the male pronucleus (B). Finally, once the sperm have fused with the oocyte, the removal of the seminal plasma proteins and glycoprotein coat prevents polyspermy (E), where one oocyte is fertilised by multiple sperm. This is because the removal of the glycoprotein coat exposes the Arrestin protein on the surface of the sperm head, which acts as a ligand for the MHC class II receptors on the surface of the oocyte. This binding stops further fusion events.  Source: 'Reproductive Biology and Pharmacology', lecture in Case 2 of the 'Reproductive System' plenary. The gag reflex is triggered by irritation of the sensory regions of the nasopharynx and oropharynx. It serves as a protective mechanism against entry into the airway of foreign objects and noxious substances. The laryngeal muscles contract powerfully, closing off the upper airway so that breathing cannot occur. The closure of the upper airway occurs before the larynx closes, which explains why food sometimes enters the windpipe and is then expelled from the mouth instead of the stomach.
